Kept from the Hour: Biblical Evidence for the Pretribulational Return of Christ
A classic defence of the pre-tribulation rapture, arguing from the promise of Revelation 3:10 and the nature of the tribulation as divine wrath.
A Systematic Theology of the Christian Religion
Two-volume systematic theology whose eschatology section argues for a rapture at the seventh, or last, trumpet in the middle of the seventieth week.
The Sign
Full statement of the prewrath system, arguing that the church is gathered after the cosmic signs and before the day of the Lord.
The Approaching Advent of Christ
A detailed posttribulational critique of the Darby school, arguing that the early church and the New Testament know only one coming after the tribulation.
The Saints' Rapture to the Presence of the Lord Jesus
A statement of the partial-rapture view, arguing that only watchful believers are taken before the tribulation.
Two Academical Exercises on Subjects Bearing the Following Titles: Millennium, Last-Novelties
Essay by a colonial Baptist pastor that places the rapture of the saints about three and a half years before the end; cited by pretribulationists as an early witness.
The Coming of Messiah in Glory and Majesty
1812 (English 1827)
A Jesuit futurist premillennial work that revived expectation of a literal reign of Christ and was translated by Edward Irving.
The Rapture and an Early Medieval Citation
Bibliotheca Sacra article presenting the Pseudo-Ephraem sermon as an early pre-tribulational statement; its reading is disputed by other scholars.
The Incredible Cover-Up
Argues that the pre-tribulation rapture originated with Margaret MacDonald in 1830 and was taken up by Darby and Irving; the claim is disputed by pretribulationists and many historians.
The Roots of Fundamentalism: British and American Millenarianism, 1800-1930
Standard history of nineteenth-century millenarianism, including Albury, Irving, Darby, the Niagara conferences and the Scofield Bible.
Maranatha: Our Lord, Come! A Definitive Study of the Rapture of the Church
A dispensational defense of the pretribulation rapture, with extended treatment of imminence and the day of the Lord.
The End: Re-thinking the Revelation
An early twentieth-century case for a rapture at the middle of the seventieth week, linked to the seventh trumpet.
A detailed presentation of the prewrath rapture view, distinguishing the great tribulation from the day of the Lord's wrath.
Entrance into the Kingdom: Reward According to Works
A Victorian English writer's case that entry into the millennial kingdom and the first rapture are rewards for faithful believers.
Original title and date vary across editions.
Firstborn Sons: Their Rights and Risks
A Brethren writer's argument for a selective rapture of watchful believers as firstborn heirs.
Die Einholung des Kyrios
A German study arguing that apantesis reflects the formal civic welcome and escort of a visiting ruler.
Hellenistic Formal Receptions and Paul's Use of APANTESIS in 1 Thessalonians 4:17
Argues in the Bulletin for Biblical Research that apantesis was not a technical term for a formal reception.
A Brief Note on "Hellenistic Formal Receptions and Paul's Use of APANTESIS in 1 Thessalonians 4:17"
A reply to Cosby defending the escort sense of apantesis in 1 Thessalonians 4:17.
Premillennialism: Why There Must Be a Future Earthly Kingdom of Jesus

A short defence of a future earthly kingdom of Christ, arguing from the Old Testament promises, the Gospels, Acts and Revelation 20 that the kingdom has a future stage on this earth after Christ's return.
The Millennial Maze: Sorting Out Evangelical Options
A survey of the main millennial views, their history and the outlook on the world each one tends to produce, written for a general Christian readership.
A Basic Guide to Eschatology: Making Sense of the Millennium
A revised edition of Erickson's Contemporary Options in Eschatology, setting out the millennial and tribulational views with their arguments and difficulties.
The Greek Testament, vol. 4 (Hebrews to Revelation)

A classic critical commentary on the Greek New Testament. Its note on Revelation 20:4-6 argues that the first resurrection must be bodily if the second is, an argument still cited by premillennialists.
Remarks on the Prophetic Visions in the Book of Daniel
A futurist study of Daniel by a Brethren-linked biblical scholar who rejected the secret rapture. It proposes reading Daniel 12:2 as describing two groups raised at different times.
First published in the 1840s-1850s in several editions; the edition year is approximate.
The Politics of Jesus
Argues that Jesus' life and cross set out a social ethic of nonviolent, servant community, so the church itself is the visible sign of God's kingdom.
Resident Aliens: Life in the Christian Colony
Calls the church a colony of heaven within a foreign culture; its first social task is to be a faithful community, not to manage society.
Living in God's Two Kingdoms: A Biblical Vision for Christianity and Culture
Sets out a Reformed two-kingdoms view: Christians serve in the common kingdom under the Noahic covenant, while the redemptive kingdom is expressed now in the church.
Lectures on Calvinism (Stone Lectures)
Kuyper's Princeton lectures present Calvinism as a life-system touching religion, politics, science and art, under Christ's lordship over every sphere.
Reformed Dogmatics, Volume 4: Holy Spirit, Church, and New Creation
Bavinck's dogmatics, translated into English; the eschatology section teaches that grace restores nature and that the new creation renews, not replaces, this world.
Creation Regained: Biblical Basics for a Reformational Worldview
A short Kuyperian account of creation, fall and redemption: redemption restores the whole created order, so every area of life can be reformed.
The Institutes of Biblical Law
A commentary on the Ten Commandments arguing that God's law, including its case laws, is the standard for personal and social life.
Theonomy in Christian Ethics
Argues from Matthew 5:17-19 that the Old Testament law continues in exhaustive detail unless the New Testament changes it, including for civil rulers.
Unconditional Surrender: God's Program for Victory
A popular introduction to Christian Reconstruction: God's sovereignty, law, and the progressive victory of the gospel in history.
Dominion! How Kingdom Action Can Change the World
Wagner argues that God commissioned believers to take dominion and transform society, naming the 'seven mountains' of culture as the arenas of that work.
Invading Babylon: The 7 Mountain Mandate
Presents the seven mountains (religion, family, education, government, media, arts and entertainment, business) as spheres believers are called to influence.
A New Apostolic Reformation? A Biblical Response to a Worldwide Movement
An evangelical critique of NAR teaching on present-day apostles and prophets and on the dominion or seven mountains mandate.
To Change the World: The Irony, Tragedy, and Possibility of Christianity in the Late Modern World
A sociologist argues that evangelical, mainline and Anabaptist strategies for 'changing the world' misread how culture changes, and proposes 'faithful presence' instead.
Whatever Happened to Heaven?
A pretribulational critique of dominion, reconstruction and Kingdom Now teaching, warning that hope has shifted from Christ's return to earthly success.
The Kingdom of Christ: The New Evangelical Perspective
Traces how covenant and dispensational theologians moved toward an 'already and not yet' kingdom, and what this means for evangelical public engagement.
Christ and Culture
A classic typology of five Christian stances toward culture, from 'Christ against culture' to 'Christ the transformer of culture'.

Christians agree that Jesus will come again, raise the dead and gather his people (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17). They disagree on three linked questions. First, when are believers 'caught up' to meet the Lord: before, in the middle of, late in, or at the end of a future time of trouble, or at one single return with no seven-year period at all? Second, what is the thousand-year reign of Revelation 20:1-6: the present age of Christ's rule from heaven (amillennial), a coming golden age of gospel success (postmillennial), or a future reign on earth after his return (historic and dispensational premillennial)? Third, what is the church's task toward God's kingdom: to wait for Christ to establish a literal kingdom at his coming, or to steward a kingdom he already established at his resurrection (Matthew 28:18-20)? Many positions sit between these two ends. This study sets out each view as its best defenders present it, with their key texts, their arguments, the strongest counters and their answers. It traces how each view arose in church history, and it closes with the common ground that all of them share.

Christ comes for his church before the seven-year tribulation begins. Believers are caught up to heaven and later return with him at his visible coming to earth. The tribulation is Daniel's seventieth week, a time of God's wrath focused on Israel and the nations. The rapture can happen at any moment, with no prophesied sign before it.

The rapture opens the seven years (0). Pretribulationists hold that the whole seventieth week is the day of the Lord, so wrath begins with the first seal (Revelation 6:1). The church is absent from all of it and returns with Christ at year 7.

Taught systematically by John Nelson Darby and the Plymouth Brethren from the 1830s. Spread in America through prophecy conferences, the Scofield Reference Bible (1909) and Dallas Theological Seminary. Proponents point to earlier hints, such as Pseudo-Ephraem and Morgan Edwards, but how much these teach the view is disputed.

It explains the promise that believers are not appointed to wrath and the call to expect Christ at any moment. It keeps the distinction between Israel and the church that dispensationalists find in Daniel 9:24-27. It notes that the church is not named on earth in Revelation 4-18.

Critics answer that no single text places the rapture before the tribulation. Jesus and Paul seem to describe one gathering after the tribulation (Matthew 24:29-31; 2 Thessalonians 2:1-3). Many see the view as a nineteenth-century development. Defenders reply that the doctrine is built from several texts together and that age does not decide truth.
Mid-tribulation rapture

The church is caught up at the midpoint of the seven years, when the Antichrist breaks his covenant (Daniel 9:27). The first half holds human and satanic trouble that the church endures. The second half, the great tribulation, is God's wrath, from which the church is removed.

The rapture comes at 3.5 years. Many link Paul's 'last trump' (1 Corinthians 15:52) with the seventh trumpet (Revelation 11:15) and the rising of the two witnesses (Revelation 11:11-12). Divine wrath fills the second half, from 3.5 to 7.

Developed in the twentieth century among premillennialists who doubted both a pre- and a post-tribulation rapture. Norman B. Harrison (1941) and J. Oliver Buswell (1962) gave it its main form. Gleason Archer defended a related view in the 1984 Three Views book.

It takes seriously the recurring half-week (time, times and half a time) in Daniel and Revelation. It accepts that the church suffers tribulation while still holding that it escapes wrath. It offers a link between the 'last trumpet' texts.

Critics from both sides note that Revelation's seventh trumpet is part of a judgment series, not a gathering signal. They argue that wrath begins earlier (the sixth seal) or later (at the return). Few current scholars defend it. Supporters answer that the midpoint is the clearest structural break in the prophecy.
Pre-wrath rapture

The church will face the Antichrist's persecution in the great tribulation. That persecution is cut short when Christ comes, after the sun, moon and stars are darkened, to gather his elect. The day of the Lord's wrath then begins and runs to the end of the seventieth week.

The rapture falls at an unknown point in the second half, shown here as about 5.25 years. It follows the cosmic signs of the sixth seal (Revelation 6:12-17; Matthew 24:29-31). God's wrath, the trumpets and bowls, begins at once after it with the seventh seal.

Formulated by Robert Van Kampen and popularised by Marvin Rosenthal, who left a pretribulational ministry and published The Pre-Wrath Rapture of the Church (1990). Van Kampen's The Sign (1992) gave the full system. Alan Kurschner and Alan Hultberg have given it academic defence.

It separates human persecution from God's wrath, as many texts do. It follows the order of Jesus' Olivet sermon closely: tribulation, cosmic signs, then gathering. It explains the great multitude that comes 'out of the great tribulation' (Revelation 7:14).

Pretribulationists argue that the seals are God's wrath from the start, since the Lamb opens them. Posttribulationists argue that Matthew 24:29-31 describes the final return, not a separate rapture. Defenders reply that the text first mentions wrath only at the sixth seal (Revelation 6:17).
Post-tribulation rapture

The church goes through the tribulation and is gathered at the single, visible return of Christ at its end. Believers rise to meet the Lord in the air and escort him back to earth, as citizens went out to meet an arriving king. God protects his people through the trouble, as he protected Israel in Egypt.

The rapture comes at year 7, at the visible return. Posttribulationists hold that God's full wrath falls on the wicked at the return itself (2 Thessalonians 1:7-9). Judgments during the tribulation fall on unbelievers while believers are kept through them (John 17:15).

Most early Christian writers, such as Irenaeus and Hippolytus, expected the church to face the Antichrist before Christ returns. In modern times it was revived against Darby by B. W. Newton, then by Alexander Reese (1937), George Eldon Ladd (1956), Robert Gundry (1973) and Douglas Moo.

It reads Jesus' and Paul's gathering texts in their most direct order. It has strong support in the early church. Its reading of the Greek word for 'meeting' (apantēsis) in 1 Thessalonians 4:17 fits the escort custom. It names one second coming, not two stages.

Pretribulationists answer that it loses the any-moment hope and leaves no unglorified believers to enter and populate the millennium. They also ask why believers are lifted up only to return at once. Posttribulationists reply that the millennium's people come from survivors who turn to Christ, and the hope is Christ's appearing, not escape.
Partial rapture

Only watchful, faithful believers are caught up before the tribulation. Other true believers, who are not ready, remain on earth to be purified and are taken later, during or at the end of it. The rapture is a reward for readiness, not a part of salvation itself.

Watchful believers are taken at the start (0), and wrath begins then. Other believers are gathered in later raptures during the seven years or at Christ's return at year 7. Proponents differ on how many stages there are.
Taught by Robert Govett in England from the 1850s, then by G. H. Pember, D. M. Panton and G. H. Lang. Watchman Nee spread the view in China. It has always been a minority view.
It takes seriously the many warnings to watch and be ready, and texts that tie being 'counted worthy' to escape (Luke 21:36). It explains why the parables include unready servants and virgins.

Critics say it divides the body of Christ, which Paul says is raised as one: 'the dead in Christ' and 'we who are alive' (1 Thessalonians 4:16-17; 1 Corinthians 15:51). They argue that it bases the rapture on works, not grace. Proponents reply that salvation is by grace, while reward and timing depend on faithfulness.
One coming, no future seven years

There is one future return of Christ, visible and glorious. At it the dead are raised, the living are changed and caught up, and the final judgment follows. Daniel's seventieth week is fulfilled in Christ's first coming or the events around AD 70, so no future seven-year tribulation exists. The church suffers tribulation throughout this age.

No future seven-year period exists, so the view has no place on this scale. The 'catching up' happens at Christ's single return at the end of history (John 6:40). Tribulation marks the whole time between Christ's two comings. God's final wrath falls at the last day.

This was the dominant view of the church from Augustine through the Reformation. It remains standard in Catholic, Orthodox, Lutheran and Reformed teaching. It is held by most amillennialists, postmillennialists and preterists.

It reads the New Testament as teaching one return, one resurrection of all and one judgment (John 5:28-29). It has the deepest history in the creeds and the church. It does not depend on a gap between Daniel's sixty-ninth and seventieth weeks.

Futurists argue that it does not explain Revelation's detailed sequence or the unique 'great tribulation' Jesus foretold (Matthew 24:21). Premillennialists argue that Revelation 20 places two resurrections a thousand years apart. Proponents reply that Revelation repeats its visions, so it does not set out a strict timeline.
Caught up to meet the Lord in the air
When believers rise to "meet" the Lord in the air, do they go with him to heaven, or do they turn and escort him back to earth?

This is the clearest rapture text. Paul gives no signs and no tribulation before it, and he offers it as comfort (verse 18). Pretribulationists hold that Christ takes the church to the Father's house (John 14:2-3) and returns with it seven years later. The word "meet" does not by itself say which way the party moves after the meeting.

Midtribulationists agree that this is a gathering to heaven, separate from the return to earth. They place it at the middle of the week, linked to the "last trumpet" of 1 Corinthians 15:52, which they connect with the seventh trumpet in Revelation 11.

Prewrath writers read this as the same event as the gathering of the elect in Matthew 24:31: the same descent, trumpet, clouds and angels. It happens after the Antichrist is revealed and the cosmic signs appear, but before God's wrath falls on the earth.

Posttribulationists stress the word apantesis. In Greek use it often described citizens going out to meet a visiting ruler and then escorting him back into the city (compare Acts 28:15). Believers rise to meet Christ and return with him at once to earth.

Partial-rapture writers agree that this is a rapture before the tribulation, but note that it is for "the dead in Christ" and those who are his. They read other texts (Luke 21:36, Hebrews 9:28) to mean that only watchful believers are taken at this stage.

Amillennial and postmillennial writers read the trumpet, the voice and the cloud as one public, visible event, the single return of Christ at the end of the age. The meeting in the air leads straight to the resurrection, the judgment and the new creation.
Not appointed to wrath
Does "God has not appointed us to wrath" mean believers are removed before the tribulation, or only that they escape God's final judgment?

Paul moves straight from the rapture (4:13-18) to "the day of the Lord" (5:1-3) and says believers are not destined for wrath. Pretribulationists hold that the whole seventieth week is the day of the Lord and is full of divine wrath (Revelation 6:16-17), so the church must be removed before it begins.

Midtribulationists say the wrath of God is poured out in the second half of the week, especially in the trumpets and bowls. The first half is the wrath of man and Satan. So the church is removed at the middle, before divine wrath begins.

Prewrath writers agree that believers are exempt from God's wrath, but separate it from the "great tribulation", which is the Antichrist's persecution. God's wrath starts only after the sixth seal (Revelation 6:17), so the church endures persecution and is rescued before the trumpets.

Posttribulationists read "wrath" as God's final judgment on the lost, contrasted with "salvation" in the same verse. God can protect his people in the midst of judgment, as he did Israel in Goshen (Exodus 8:22). The verse promises rescue from wrath, not removal from trouble.
Partial-rapture writers say the promise holds for those who are watchful and sober (5:6-8). Believers who are spiritually asleep may face part of the time of testing, though not eternal wrath.

On this view the wrath is the final judgment at Christ's one return. Paul's contrast is between eternal wrath and eternal salvation through Christ (compare 1 Thessalonians 1:10), not between two stages of future history.
The last trumpet
Is the "last trumpet" the last trumpet of all, the seventh trumpet of Revelation, or simply the signal that closes the church age?

Pretribulationists say "last" means the final trumpet for the church, a call to gather God's people, as in the Roman army or Israel's camp (Numbers 10:2-6). It need not be the last trumpet in all prophecy, and Paul wrote before Revelation's trumpets were known.

Midtribulationists identify Paul's last trumpet with the seventh trumpet (Revelation 11:15), which they place near the middle of the week. At that trumpet the kingdom is announced and the dead are judged and rewarded (Revelation 11:18).

Prewrath writers usually do not equate this trumpet with the seventh trumpet of Revelation. They link it to the trumpet that gathers the elect in Matthew 24:31, sounded after the cosmic signs and before the day of the Lord's wrath.

Posttribulationists take "last" at face value. If it is the last trumpet, it cannot sound seven years before other trumpets. They link it with the great trumpet of Matthew 24:31, which is clearly after the tribulation.
Partial-rapture writers accept a rapture at a trumpet but hold that later raptures of other believers can still occur during the tribulation. They give less weight to the word "last".

On this view the last trumpet ends history. It sounds once, at the single coming, when all the dead are raised and the living changed. Nothing in the passage suggests further trumpets or a later stage.
I will come again and receive you
Does Jesus promise to take his people to the Father's house in heaven, or to come and dwell with them?

Pretribulationists see a clear sequence: Jesus goes to prepare a place, comes back, and takes his disciples to where he is, the Father's house. This fits a coming for the church that takes it to heaven, not a coming to earth to set up the kingdom.
Midtribulationists share the pretribulational reading: the church is taken to heaven while judgment falls on the earth in the second half of the week.
Prewrath writers agree that Jesus takes his people to be with him. They note the text gives no timing, and they place the event after the sixth seal.

Posttribulationists reply that the text says nothing about a seven-year stay in heaven. "Where I am" can mean with Christ wherever he is. In John 14:23 the Father and Son come to make their home with believers, which points to God dwelling with his people, not a removal.

Many in this group read the "rooms" as a place with God secured by Christ's death and resurrection. Some see a present fulfilment in the Spirit's coming (John 14:18, 14:23); all see a final fulfilment at the one return, ending in the new creation where God dwells with his people (Revelation 21:3).
Kept from the hour of trial
Does "keep you from (tereo ek) the hour of trial" mean removal before the hour, or protection through it?

The promise is to be kept from the hour itself, not just the trial. Pretribulationists argue that the only way to be kept from a period of time that comes on the whole world is to be removed from it. The hour is world-wide and aimed at "those who dwell on the earth".
Midtribulationists apply the promise to the hour of God's wrath in the second half of the week. The church is kept from that hour by a rapture at the middle.
Prewrath writers say the hour of trial is the day of the Lord's wrath, which begins after the sixth seal. The church is kept from that hour by being gathered just before it.

Gundry and others note that the same phrase "keep from" (tereo ek) is used in John 17:15, where Jesus asks the Father not to take his disciples out of the world but to keep them from the evil one. So it means protection while present, not removal.
Partial-rapture writers stress that the promise is a reward: "because you have kept my word". Only faithful, watchful believers are kept from the hour. This is a main text for their view.

On this view the promise was first to the church at Philadelphia, facing a real trial in its own day. It also teaches that God guards his people spiritually in every trial. It does not describe a future seven-year period.
"Come up here" and the church in chapters 4-19
Does John's call to "come up here" picture the rapture, and is the church truly absent from Revelation 4-19?

The word "church" appears nineteen times in chapters 1-3 and not again until 22:16. Pretribulationists read this as a sign that the church is in heaven during the judgments of chapters 6-19. Many see the twenty-four elders (4:4) as the raptured church, crowned and enthroned. Most do not claim that 4:1 itself is the rapture.
Midtribulationists agree the church is in heaven during the later judgments, but place its arrival at chapter 11 rather than chapter 4.
Prewrath writers say the church is on earth during the seals and is seen as the great multitude arriving in heaven in 7:9-14, "out of the great tribulation", just before the trumpets.

Posttribulationists reply that "come up here" is said to John alone, as a prophet. The word "church" is also missing from many New Testament books and from heaven in chapters 4-19. Saints, servants, and those who keep the commands of God and the testimony of Jesus (12:17) appear on earth throughout.

Amillennial writers see chapter 4 as a new vision of the throne room that frames the whole age. Revelation repeats the same period from different angles, so the saints on earth in chapters 6-19 are the church in every generation.
The gathering, the apostasy and the restrainer
Must the apostasy and the man of lawlessness come before "our gathering together to him", and who is the restrainer?

Paul calms readers who feared they were already in the day of the Lord. Pretribulationists say the restrainer is the Holy Spirit acting through the church, so the church is removed before the lawless one is revealed. Some also read "the falling away" (apostasia) as "the departure", meaning the rapture itself.
Midtribulationists place the revealing of the man of lawlessness in the first half of the week, before the church is gathered at the middle.

Prewrath writers say Paul plainly puts the apostasy and the revealing of the man of lawlessness before the day of the Lord and the gathering. Kurschner argues that believers will see the Antichrist's rise before they are gathered.

Posttribulationists say the "coming" and "gathering" of verse 1 are the same event as the coming that destroys the lawless one (verse 8). The church will see him first. They take the restrainer to be something else, such as God's ordering of the state or the preaching of the gospel.
